title: What numbers do the old Sanskrit names stand for?
description: The five old names eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta sit in a row, and each fills an empty box with its number. Every step multiplies the number before by ten. Keeko's doubt is that each name is ten more than the one before.
teaching_notes: One idea: each old name is ten times the one before, so the names follow the powers of ten we still say. Watch for students who think each name is ten more than the last.

source: The Yajurveda lists eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta. Wh
video_script.why: The child sees that the old Indian number names grow by multiplying by ten each time, the same powers of ten we use when we say numbers today.
video_script.substitution: Write the number under each name and compare each one with the one before it.
video_script.anchor: the row of five old number names from the Yajurveda, with an empty box under each
video_script.wrong_answer: each name is ten more than the one before
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds ten to get from one name to the next. Ten more than one is eleven, not ten, so the rule fails at the very first step.
video_script.payoff_line: Each name is ten times the one before

final_answer.value: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before
final_answer.spoken: one, ten, one hundred, one thousand and ten thousand, each ten times the one before

hold_back: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before
never_show: the answer card before the last beat of the board solution
maths_rules: each name is 10 times the one before, so the names follow the powers of 10
the rule add ten fails at the first step: 1 + 10 = 11, not 10
video_script.design: One idea: each name is ten times the one before. The row of names stays all video; the empty boxes fill one by one.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the oldest number names.
<bookmark mark='names'/>An ancient Indian text, the Yajurveda, lists eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which numbers are these, and how is each one related to the one before it?

marks.eka: 1 appears under eka and 10 under dasha, with ten small lamps

narration: <bookmark mark='row'/>Put the five names in a row, in the order the text gives them.
<bookmark mark='eka'/>Eka is the name for one, and dasha is the name for ten.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The other three names get empty boxes, waiting for their numbers.

beats.on_screen: Given: the names eka, dasha, shata, sahasra, ayuta, in this order

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find each number, and how each one grows from the one before.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: dasha = 10 × eka = 10 × 1 = 10; an arrow marked × 10 joins eka to dasha

marks.m1: 10 × 1 = 10 is written under dasha with an arrow from eka

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, compare dasha with eka.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Dasha is ten ones, so multiply ten by one, which gives ten.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: shata = 10 × dasha = 10 × 10 = 100; an arrow marked × 10 joins dasha to shata

marks.m2: 10 × 10 = 100 fills the box under shata with an arrow from dasha

narration: <bookmark mark='s2'/>Step two, compare shata with dasha.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Shata is ten groups of ten, so multiply ten by ten, which gives one hundred.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: sahasra = 10 × shata = 10 × 100 = 1000; an arrow marked × 10 joins shata to sahasra

marks.m3: 10 × 100 = 1000 fills the box under sahasra with an arrow from shata

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, compare sahasra with shata.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Sahasra is ten groups of one hundred, so multiply ten by one hundred, which gives one thousand.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: ayuta = 10 × sahasra = 10 × 1000 = 10000; an arrow marked × 10 joins sahasra to ayuta

marks.m4: 10 × 1000 = 10000 fills the box under ayuta with an arrow from sahasra

narration: <bookmark mark='s4'/>Step four, compare ayuta with sahasra.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Ayuta is ten groups of one thousand, so multiply ten by one thousand, which gives ten thousand.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Each name is ten times the one before.
<bookmark mark='nums'/>The names stand for one, ten, one hundred, one thousand and ten thousand.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows + 10 under each arrow; next to eka and dasha, 1 + 10 = 11 is written beside the 10; the bubble is struck through; × 10 returns under each arrow

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows the rule add ten
marks.test: 1 + 10 = 11 is written next to the 10 of dasha and the two do not match
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and × 10 returns under each arrow

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks each name is ten more than the one before.
<bookmark mark='test'/>Test it on the first step. Ten more than one is eleven.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But dasha is ten, so adding ten cannot be the rule.
We multiply by ten each time.
